report:
**Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by evidence.**

Multiple large studies and meta-analyses confirm that bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR improves survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared with no bystander CPR at all. The American Heart Association's scientific advisory notes that "hands-only (compression-only) CPR was better than no attempt at CPR and produced survival equivalent to conventional CPR" in the cited bystander studies (ahajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.107.189380). A landmark Swedish nationwide registry study of witnessed OHCA found that patients receiving either standard or hands-only CPR were roughly twice as likely to survive 30 days compared with those receiving no CPR, across all time periods studied (as reported via emergency-live.com, summarizing the Circulation/AHA-published Swedish data).

This is corroborated by randomized and meta-analytic evidence comparing compression-only to standard CPR: the Lancet meta-analysis found that dispatcher-assisted compression-only CPR was associated with *improved* survival compared to standard CPR with ventilations (thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(10)61454-7), and the NEJM trial found a modestly higher 30-day survival with compression-only CPR (8.7%) versus standard CPR (7.0%) (nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0908991). Since standard CPR itself is well established as superior to no CPR, and compression-only performs at least as well as (often better than) standard CPR in adult OHCA, the chain of evidence supports that hands-only CPR confers a substantial survival benefit over no bystander CPR.

Caveats: benefits are somewhat smaller in pediatric/asphyxial arrests, where conventional CPR with ventilations may be preferable, and outcome magnitude varies by study design and population.
